teaser: A kiss, two thefts, and a pretty girl with a scorpion's tail. A royal riddle in ice-cold paint.
review_notes:
Painted c. 1545, probably for Cosimo I de' Medici as a diplomatic gift to King Francis I of France (per Vasari); oil on wood, about 146 x 116 cm.
Bought by the National Gallery in 1860; Venus's tongue and nipple and other areas were overpainted in the 19th century and uncovered in a 1958 cleaning (please verify date).
Identities are debated: howling figure = Jealousy, or the effects of syphilis (Conway, 1986); top-left = Oblivion (or Fraud/Night); girl with honeycomb = Fraud/Deceit (or Pleasure). Lesson presents them as readings.
Girl's hands are reversed (right hand on left arm): standard observation.
Blue background described as ultramarine from lapis lazuli: verify with NG technical notes.
Monty Python's Flying Circus foot: Terry Gilliam took Cupid's foot from this painting.
Folly's right foot stepping on thorns and the bells on his anklet: standard descriptions, thorns not clearly legible in this image.

lesson.text: A mother and son are kissing, tenderly, eyes half closed. While they kiss, she is slipping an arrow out of his quiver, and his fingers are lifting the crown off her head. Affection and robbery in the same gesture: that is the temperature of this whole picture.

She is Venus, goddess of love. He is Cupid, her son, the winged boy whose arrows make people fall in love. Around 1545 Agnolo Bronzino, court painter to Duke Cosimo de' Medici in Florence, packed them into a panel with six other characters and not one clear explanation.

The painting was most likely a diplomatic present from the duke to Francis I, king of France, a ruler famous for loving Italian art and erotic wit. It was made to be decoded slowly, by a few people, in a private room. It was a conversation piece in the most literal sense.

lesson.title: The double theft
lesson.text: Start with the couple in the middle and follow their hands.

spots.title: The kiss
spots.text: Lips meet, and if you look at her mouth you can see the tip of her tongue. For a goddess and her own son, it is deliberately uncomfortable.

spots.title: The stolen arrow
spots.text: Her raised right hand holds one of his golden arrows by the shaft, drawn away while he is distracted. She is disarming the god of desire.

spots.title: The crown
spots.text: His hand cradles her head, fingers closing on the jeweled crown in her hair. He is taking something too.

spots.title: The golden apple
spots.text: In her other hand: the apple awarded to Venus as the most beautiful goddess, the prize that set off the Trojan War. Beauty's trophy, with a bad history.

lesson.text: So the central pair is a trap dressed as a caress. Everything around them develops that idea. The figures at the edges are allegories, meaning ideas given a human body: Time, Folly, Jealousy and so on. Reading them is like reading labels that have fallen off.

The skin looks like polished marble for a reason. Bronzino blended his paint until no brushstroke showed, a finish so smooth that his figures seem carved and then tinted. He was also a published poet, fond of jokes with double meanings.

On the right, a laughing child strides in with a fistful of roses to throw. He is usually called Folly or Foolish Pleasure. He is so pleased with himself that he has not noticed what is under his right foot. And he hides the strangest character of all.
Behind the laughing boy there is a sweet face that does not match its body. Where is she?

spots.title: The girl who is not a girl
spots.text: A lovely face with pearls in her hair. Follow it down: a green dress, then scales, a coiled tail and lion's paws. She is usually read as Fraud, or Deceit: charming at the top, monstrous below.

lesson.text: Her hands finish the lesson. One offers a honeycomb, the other hides the sting at the end of her tail. And they are switched: the hand on her left arm is a right hand, the other a left. What she seems to give you with one hand, she gives with the wrong one. You will see them in a moment.
Now lift your eyes to the top. The whole scene is happening in front of a blue cloth, and two figures are fighting over it.

lesson.title: The curtain
lesson.text: Someone wants this scene exposed. Someone else wants it covered.

spots.title: Father Time
spots.text: A bald, bearded old man with a furious stare and a muscular arm hauls the blue drape across. He has wings, and an hourglass rests on his shoulder at the top edge. Time reveals everything in the end.

spots.title: The hollow head
spots.text: Opposite him a figure grips the cloth too. Seen in profile, the head is a shell: a face like a mask with nothing behind it. It is often called Oblivion, forgetting, who would rather keep things hidden.

spots.title: The howler
spots.text: Below, a dark figure tears at its own hair and screams. Long read as Jealousy. Some doctors and historians see the symptoms of syphilis, a new and terrifying disease in the 1500s.

lesson.text: Put the cast together and a moral appears, though nobody can prove it is the right one: love's pleasures come with deceit, pain follows them, and time will show the bill. A sermon, then? Hardly. The picture enjoys the pleasures far too much to be a warning.
An allegory tells an idea through characters. Bronzino's version is built to be argued over: five centuries on, scholars still disagree about who half these figures are.

In 1860 the National Gallery in London bought the panel, and Victorian taste found it too much. Venus's tongue and nipple were painted over, and a veil was added across her lap. The additions were removed in a cleaning a century later.

There is also the matter of money. That intense blue behind the figures is ultramarine, a pigment ground from lapis lazuli, a stone carried from mines in what is now Afghanistan. It cost more than gold. A gift for a king had to look like one.

The cold is the last contradiction. This is a picture about desire with no warmth in it: hard light, enamel colors, bodies as pale as porcelain. Mannerism, the courtly style Bronzino mastered, preferred artifice to nature, and here artifice is the message. Nothing in love's theater is what it seems.

spots.title: Honeycomb
spots.text: The sweet gift, held out toward Venus in a hand that sits on the wrong arm.

spots.title: The sting
spots.text: Her other hand, pulled back behind the boy, holds the barbed tip of her own tail. Sweetness in front, poison behind.

spots.title: Paws and scales
spots.text: Under the green silk: a scaly, snake-like body and the hind legs of a lion. The pretty face belongs to this.

spots.title: Two masks
spots.text: Theater masks lie on the ground, one young, one old and grimacing. Masks mean disguise. They stare up with empty eyes.

spots.title: Dove and foot
spots.text: Venus's sacred bird sits under Cupid's bare foot. Terry Gilliam borrowed this foot for the giant one that stomps down in the titles of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

spots.title: Roses
spots.text: Folly is about to shower the lovers with pink roses. His grin says he sees no danger at all.

spots.title: Anklet
spots.text: A band of little bells circles the boy's ankle, the jingle of a jester. Nearby his other foot comes down on thorns, and he does not even flinch.

spots.title: The pink cushion
spots.text: Cupid kneels on a silk cushion, a symbol of ease and luxury. His pose pushes his backside toward you, one more piece of calculated cheek.

lesson.text: The painting has had many titles. The museum now calls it simply “An Allegory with Venus and Cupid,” because every more specific name takes a side in an argument that is not over.

quiz.question: What is Venus doing while she kisses Cupid?
quiz.explanation: She slips an arrow away while he lifts her crown: a double theft.

quiz.question: For whom was the painting most likely made?
options: Francis I, king of France, as a gift from Cosimo de' Medici
quiz.explanation: It was probably a diplomatic present from the duke of Florence to the French king.

quiz.question: What is wrong with the pretty girl behind Folly?
options: She has a scaly body, lion's paws and switched hands
quiz.explanation: Her sweet face sits on a monster's body, which is why she is read as Fraud.

quiz.question: How can you recognize Father Time?
quiz.explanation: The bald old man has wings and an hourglass on his shoulder.

quiz.question: What did Victorian restorers do to the painting?
options: Painted over Venus's tongue and nipple and added a veil
quiz.explanation: Details judged indecent were covered and only uncovered a century later.

quiz.question: Why was the blue background so expensive?
options: It is ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli
quiz.explanation: Ultramarine was ground from lapis lazuli and cost more than gold.

facts.text: Scholars agree on the identity of every figure in the painting.
facts.explanation: Several figures, such as the howling one and the hollow head, are still debated.

facts.text: Bronzino blended his paint so smoothly that no brushstrokes show.
facts.explanation: That polished finish makes his figures look like tinted marble.

facts.text: The foot in the Monty Python titles was taken from this painting.
facts.explanation: Terry Gilliam borrowed Cupid's foot from the lower left corner.
